question: A marketing operations specialist has built a workflow that will send Claude-drafted emails automatically to a fifty-thousand-person customer list at six tomorrow morning. Nobody has read any of the drafts yet. What should she do first?
options: A) Read the first and last few drafts as a sample, and let the send run if those ones look fine.
B) Turn off the automatic send, so that nothing reaches the list until it has been reviewed.
C) Read as many of the drafts as she can before six, and let the rest of them go out unread.
D) Ask Claude to check its own drafts overnight and correct any problems that it finds in them.
correct_answers: B) Turn off the automatic send, so that nothing reaches the list until it has been reviewed.
explanations: A sample of the first and last few tells her nothing about the drafts in between, and every one of them still goes to a real customer. Sampling is reasonable for low-stakes internal work, not for an irreversible mass send.

Correct. The output is externally visible, irreversible once sent and has a very wide blast radius, so the first move is to remove the deadline pressure by stopping the automatic send. Review can then happen properly rather than against a clock she does not control.
This accepts that unreviewed messages will reach customers anyway. Once an email is sent to fifty thousand people it cannot be recalled, so partial review under a running clock is not enough.
Leaving the model to check itself keeps the unreviewed send in place. No human has looked at anything, which is precisely the risk here.
